title: The ten who came back afraid

hook.say: before the story, can i ask you something? is there something you’d find hard to face alone, but easier with people around you?
options: then this one will feel close. listen.
then you’ll understand these scouts. listen.
fair. listen anyway, it might surprise you.

steps.line: After the escape from Egypt, Moses sent twelve scouts ahead, one from each tribe, to explore the land of Canaan. They walked it for forty days.
They came back carrying fruit: pomegranates, figs, and one cluster of grapes so big it took two men and a pole to carry it.

steps.q: The land is full of fruit. What do you think most of the scouts report?
o: Rich land, but we can’t win
Poor land, not worth a war
Holy land, not ours to take
steps.why: Ten of the twelve admitted the land flowed with milk and honey. Then came the “but”: the people were too strong (Numbers 13:27-28).

steps.line: But ten of them said the cities were walled and the people were giants. “We were in our own sight as grasshoppers, and so we were in their sight.”

steps.q: “We were grasshoppers in our own sight, and so we were in theirs.” What did the rabbis notice about the second half?
o: The scouts had no way of knowing it
Grasshoppers were a sign of a curse
They had been spotted and chased
steps.why: A midrash imagines God saying: call yourselves grasshoppers if you like, but who told you how you looked to them? The fear came from inside.

steps.line: That night, the whole people wept. Only two, Joshua and Caleb, stood up and said, “The land is an exceeding good land.”

steps.q: Same land, same giants. What did Joshua and Caleb count on that the ten didn’t?
o: A secret way into the cities
That the Lord was with them
That the giants were fewer than said
steps.why: Numbers 14:9: “The Lord is with us; do not fear them.” The ten counted the giants. The two counted God too.

steps.line: Later in the story, God calls those ten “this evil congregation.” The rabbis noticed: ten people were called a congregation. So ten became the smallest community in Jewish law.
steps.label: a teaching of the rabbis

steps.q: The people sided with the ten and refused to go. What did it cost them?
o: A year’s delay, to train an army
Forty years, a year per scouting day
Moses lost his place as leader
steps.why: Numbers 14:34. That generation never entered the land; their children did, led by Joshua and Caleb.

steps.line: Today, some prayers need a minyan of ten, like the reading from the Torah scroll and the mourner’s Kaddish. A mourner doesn’t say it alone. Nine others come.
steps.label: today

steps.line: Who counts differs. In Orthodox communities, a minyan is ten men, thirteen and older. In Reform, Reconstructionist and egalitarian Conservative ones, women count equally.
steps.label: today

say: here’s what i love. a person can pray alone, anywhere, and jews do. but some prayers speak as a public, and they need the ten.

by custom, a mourner says kaddish every day for eleven months after losing a parent. so every day, nine people show up, and grief is never carried in an empty room. the tenth doesn’t even need to know the words. being there counts.

steps.q: The ten scouts were afraid, and the rabbis still took a holy number from them. What does that suggest about a minyan?
o: You have to be brave to be counted
steps.why: No one has to be a hero to count. You just have to show up, and the ten become a community.

today.say: if someone you know is grieving, think about showing up once at the prayers in their home or synagogue, even if you don’t know the words. who counts in the ten depends on the community, but anyone can stand with a mourner. you can watch, learn or join in.
options: then you’re the tenth. that’s everything.
a message to someone grieving counts too.

Numbers 14:1, 6–7 (the people wept that night; Joshua and Caleb: “The land… is an exceeding good land,” JPS 1917, shortened); Numbers 14:27 (“this evil congregation,” JPS 1917)
Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 23b and Berakhot 21b (a ‘congregation’ is ten, learned from the spies; matters of holiness need ten)
Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 6a; Mishnah Avot 3:6 (the divine presence among ten)
Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De‘ah 376:4 with the Rema (the custom of saying Kaddish for eleven months)
